label: Chapter 3: Capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands, 1430 to 1568

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In 1430, Brussels hits the jackpot.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It does. The duchy of Brabant passes to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, one of the richest and most glamorous princes in Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Philip makes a choice that changes the city's destiny.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Out of all his great towns, he chooses Brussels as his main residence.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Why does that matter so much? What was the Burgundian state?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It wasn't a kingdom on a map the way we think of kingdoms.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a patchwork of territories collected through marriage, inheritance, and purchase: Flanders, Brabant, Holland, Hainaut, and soon the duchy of Luxembourg, which Philip took in 1443, as we heard in the Luxembourg episode.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So roughly modern Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Plus a good slice of northern France.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philip ruled them from a court that was the most dazzling in Europe, full of knights, painters, musicians, and diplomats.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1430, the same year he inherited Brabant, he founded a famous chivalric brotherhood, the Order of the Golden Fleece.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the heart of that court was Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More and more. The dukes lived at the Coudenberg Palace, on the hill above the town, which they enlarged into a huge complex of halls, chapels, and courtyards.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Government offices followed the court.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Money followed the offices. Artists and craftsmen followed the money.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Let's talk about the art, because this is a golden age.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The art of this period is extraordinary.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1436, the city appointed a painter named Rogier van der Weyden as its official city painter.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He was born in Tournai and trained there, and he became one of the great masters of what we now call Early Netherlandish painting.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: His portraits have those sharp, searching faces.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And emotional religious scenes, admired across Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the town hall, he painted a series of panels about justice, scenes of rulers hearing the cases of ordinary people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Those paintings were destroyed in 1695, but the artist's reputation lived on.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Rogier is buried in the cathedral of Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then there's tapestry.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels became famous for it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Weavers in the city produced huge, richly colored wall hangings, made of wool, silk, and threads of gold and silver.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Tapestries were the luxury art of the age, and a prince would pay more for a fine set than for a painting.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I remember the Sistine Chapel connection.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the second decade of the sixteenth century, Pope Leo the Tenth commissioned a set of tapestries for the Sistine Chapel, based on designs by Raphael, and the weaving was done in Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The city soon introduced a quality mark, a pair of the letter B around a red shield, woven into the edge of authentic pieces to protect the brand.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A brand mark, in the fifteen hundreds.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Very modern.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Very. But the Burgundian dream ended abruptly in 1477.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philip's grandson, Charles the Bold, was killed fighting the Swiss and Lorrainers outside the city of Nancy, leaving a single daughter, Mary of Burgundy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who had been born in Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And she was the most eligible heiress in Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She married Maximilian of Habsburg, an Austrian prince who would become Holy Roman Emperor, and when she died in a riding accident in 1482, her lands passed to their children.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Through that marriage, the Burgundian Netherlands fell into the hands of the Habsburgs, the most powerful dynasty of the next three centuries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Habsburg who matters most for Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Mary's grandson, Charles. He was born in Ghent in the year 1500, but he was raised in the Netherlands, and he saw Brussels as home.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When he was six, he inherited the Burgundian lands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1516, he was proclaimed King of Spain in a ceremony in the church of Saint Gudula in Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1519, he was elected Holy Roman Emperor, as Charles the Fifth.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Ruler of an enormous empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: From Spain and Italy to Germany, the Netherlands, and the new Spanish colonies in the Americas.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But he can't have been in Brussels very often.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Charles was usually traveling, so he needed trusted regents to govern the Netherlands in his absence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His aunt Margaret of Austria ruled from nearby Mechelen.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Later, his sister Mary of Hungary took over, and in 1531 the central government institutions were fixed in Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So that's the moment it becomes the capital of the Low Countries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A role it has kept, in one form or another, ever since.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it's a brilliant time intellectually.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. In 1521, the great humanist Erasmus of Rotterdam, the most famous scholar in Europe, spent several months in Anderlecht, then a village outside Brussels, living in a house you can visit today as a museum.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Vesalius was a Brussels boy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Andreas Vesalius, born in Brussels in 1514.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He grew up to be a pioneer of modern anatomy, and his groundbreaking book on the structure of the human body, published in 1543, corrected centuries of errors by examining real corpses.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Bruegel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1563, the great painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder moved to Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He married the daughter of a well-known local artist, and in the remaining years of his short life he painted some of his most famous scenes of peasant life and village feasts.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He died in Brussels in 1569 and was buried in a church in the Marolles district.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Charles left another mark on the city, didn't he?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A festival.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1549, there was a great festival in Brussels to present his son and heir, Philip, to the people of the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The procession of guilds, nobles, and giant figures that wound through the streets is remembered today in a summer pageant called the Ommegang, held every year on the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then the abdication. That's such a scene.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In October of 1555, in the great hall of the Coudenberg Palace, Charles gave up his crown.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exhausted, ill, and weary of rule, he announced that he was handing the Netherlands over to Philip the Second.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Witnesses recorded that he leaned on the shoulder of a young nobleman, the twenty-two-year-old William of Orange, and that the hall wept as he spoke.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then he retired to a monastery.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Soon afterward he handed Spain over too, and yes, retired to a monastery.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the picture isn't all golden, is it?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Reformation arrives.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By now Brussels was a city of tens of thousands of people, a great center of government, art, and trade.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But dark clouds were on the horizon.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther had challenged the Catholic Church, and the new Protestant ideas spread quickly through the Low Countries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the authorities reacted.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1523, in the very center of Brussels, two young Augustinian monks, Henry Voes and Johannes van den Esschen, were burned at the stake on the Grand Place for refusing to renounce Luther's teachings.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They're considered the first martyrs of the Protestant Reformation.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a sign of things to come.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the new ruler?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philip the Second was a devoutly Catholic king who lived in Spain and never really understood the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He intended to stamp out heresy, enforce Catholic orthodoxy, and tighten royal control over the proud cities.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the cities, with their ancient privileges, weren't going to take that lying down.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not without a fight.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: If someone wants to touch this chapter, where do they go?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Place Royale, at the top of the hill.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Under the square, an archaeological site called the Coudenberg lets you walk through the surviving cellars and streets of the old ducal palace.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'll be walking the same ground where Charles the Fifth gave up the biggest empire in the world.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Next time, revolt, execution, bombardment, and an elegant rebuilding.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A busy century and a half.
